case_name: Ross v. New Brunswick Teachers' Association and Beutel
text:
IN THE COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH OF NEW
BRUNSWICK

TRIAL DIVISION

JUDICIAL
DISTRICT OF MONCTON

Date:
19960327

Docket:
M/C/423/94

BETWEEN:

MALCOLM ROSS,

Plaintiff,

-and-

NEW BRUNSWICK TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION
and JOSH BEUTEL

Defendants.

BEFORE:                                                 The
Honourable Mr. Justice Paul S. Creaghan

AT:                                                            Moncton,
New Brunswick

DATE
OF HEARING:                             March 25, 1996

DATE
OF DECISION:                            March 27, 1996

APPEARANCES
:

John
D. Hughes for the Plaintiff

Richard A. Williams for the Defendant,
New Brunswick Teachers' Association

David
M. Lutz, Q.C. for the Defendant, Josh Beutel

CREAGHAN, J.

The Defendants seek a ruling with
respect to the propriety of a question asked on Examination for Discovery
pursuant to Rule 33.10(2)(c).

The Plaintiff alleges that he was
defamed by the Defendants by holding him up to contempt and ridicule in part by
depicting him as anti-Semitic. The Defendants in part plead fair comment.

The Plaintiff admits that he is the
author of a booklet entitled "The Real Holocaust". The cover of the
booklet features a drawing that is obviously directed to the author's views
opposing abortion. The Defendants maintain that the drawing might also be
interpreted as anti-Semitic.

On Examination for Discovery, the
Plaintiff stated that he as the author of the booklet took full responsibility
for the drawing on the cover and what it should be taken to mean.

The Defendants asked the
Plaintiff to identify the person who made the drawing on the cover of "The
Real Holocaust". The Plaintiff refused to answer on the grounds that the
name of the person who made the drawing is not relevant to the present action
and therefore not a proper question that he is required to answer.

[Page
2]

The Defendants argue that
the drawing is anti-Semitic. They suggest that the sinister figure admitted to
give people a visual concept of evil, is anti-Semitic because it is intended to
depict Dr. Henry Morgantaler who is a Jew, and it draws an analogy to the
Jewish king Herod and the biblical account of his instruction to kill all first
born babies at the time of the birth of Christ. As such, it is argued that the
drawing shows the disposition of the Plaintiff as anti-Semitic.

Accordingly, the Defendants
maintain that the person who made the drawing may be in a position to confirm
the purport of the drawing and relate it to his understanding of the intent and
disposition of the Plaintiff in publishing the booklet.

It is beyond the purport of
this motion for me to weigh the merit of this argument. Clearly, the principal
thrust of the drawing is to state an anti-abortion position. As to whether it
also should be taken to depict anti-Semitic sentiment is tenuous but arguable.

The disposition of the Plaintiff in this
latter aspect is relevant to this action. To the extent that the person who
made the drawing might be in a position to comment as to the Plaintiff's
disposition discerned from his instructions from the Plaintiff upon making the
drawing for the cover of the booklet, his testimony would be relevant. If the
author's intentions were designed to

[Page 3]

express opposition to abortion, with or
indeed without overtones of anti-Semitism, it seems to me such testimony could
have some relevance.

Addressing the question of the latitude
that should be given to relevancy on discovery, Mr. Justice Jones of this Court
stated in
Slattery (Bankrupt) v. Slattery et al.

(1989),
1989 CanLII 7844 (NB QB)
,
95 N.B.R.(2d)
422
, at pp. 430,
431:

"Courts have generally given a wide
interpretation to relevancy. In
Marriott v. Chamberlain
(1886),
17
Q.B.D. 154
, Lord Esher, M.R., dealing with the English
Rules
which used
the phrase 'relating to any matter in question', a phrase which is certainly no
wider than that in our present
Rules
, stated:

‘But with these exceptions it seems to
me that pretty nearly anything that is material may now be asked. The right to
interrogate is not confined to the facts directly in issue, but extends to any
facts the existence or nonexistence of which is relevant to the existence or
nonexistence of the facts directly in issue.’"

Having addressed the question of
relevancy, specific to this motion Rule 32.06(2) provides:

"A party being examined for
discovery shall answer, to the best of his knowledge, information and belief,
any question concerning the names and addresses of potential witnesses."

[Page
4]

Accordingly, I find the
question to be a proper one and the Plaintiff should answer it.

Costs on this motion will
be costs in the cause.

[S]

Judge
of the Court of Queen’s Bench of New Brunswick

Moncton,
N. B.

March
27, 1996
